name: Egyptian Old Kingdom Sculpture
d: Rigid, frontal royal statues and the Great Sphinx projected pharaonic divine order in hard, eternal stone; proportion canons fixed the human figure for millennia.
w: Great Sphinx of Giza, c. 2500 BCE

name: Egyptian Middle Kingdom Sculpture
d: After the First Intermediate collapse, sculptors turned to careworn, psychologically searching royal portraits, most famously the furrowed brow of Senusret III.
w: Statue of Senusret III, c. 1850 BCE

name: Egyptian New Kingdom Tomb Painting
d: Vividly colored tomb and papyrus paintings guided the dead through the afterlife with flattened, hieroglyph-like figures moving in registers across gold-ground walls.
w: Tomb of Nefertari murals, c. 1255 BCE
Book of the Dead of Hunefer, c. 1275 BCE
Tomb of Nakht paintings, c. 1400 BCE

name: Amarna Art
d: Under Akhenaten's religious revolution, artists abandoned rigid canon for elongated, naturalistic, almost caricatured royal bodies bathed in the rays of the sun-disc Aten.
w: Amarna royal family relief, c. 1350 BCE

name: Sumerian Sculpture
d: Wide-eyed votive figures with clasped hands stood in temples in perpetual prayer for their donors, while royal tombs at Ur yielded inlaid harps and gold treasures.
w: Votive statues of Eshnunna, c. 2700 BCE

name: Akkadian Sculpture
d: The world's first empire commissioned a new heroic naturalism: the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin shows a god-king trampling enemies beneath a mountain of triumph.
w: Victory Stele of Naram-Sin, c. 2230 BCE
Bronze Head of an Akkadian Ruler, c. 2250 BCE

name: Babylonian Glazed Brickwork
d: From Hammurabi's law stele to Nebuchadnezzar's Ishtar Gate, Babylon paired legal and religious authority with glazed cobalt-blue brick reliefs of striding dragons and bulls.

name: Neo-Assyrian Relief Sculpture
d: Palace walls at Nineveh and Nimrud were lined with gypsum reliefs of royal lion hunts and military campaigns, guarded by colossal winged lamassu bulls at every gate.
w: Lion Hunt reliefs of Ashurbanipal, c. 645 BCE
Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, 825 BCE

name: Indus Valley Sculpture and Seals
d: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa produced enigmatic small-scale masterworks - a bronze dancing girl and a steatite 'priest-king' bust - alongside thousands of carved animal seals never fully deciphered.
w: Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro, c. 2300 BCE

name: Cycladic Figurines
d: Pared-down white marble figures with folded arms, likely tied to funerary ritual, look startlingly modern and later inspired Brancusi and Modigliani.
w: Marble female figure, Early Cycladic II
Harp Player of Keros, c. 2700 BCE

name: Minoan Fresco Painting
d: Palace walls at Knossos and the buried town of Akrotiri burst with buoyant, curvilinear frescoes of leaping bulls, blue monkeys, and saffron gatherers, painted with no ground line or horizon.

name: Mycenaean Gold and Shaft Grave Objects
d: Warrior kings were buried with beaten gold death masks, inlaid bronze daggers, and rock-crystal vessels, projecting martial wealth quite unlike the airy Minoan world they absorbed.
w: Lion Gate relief, Mycenae, c. 1250 BCE

name: Greek Geometric Vase Painting
d: Huge Attic grave-markers were banded with meanders, key-patterns, and rows of stick-limbed mourners and funeral processions, the first narrative figure painting in Greek art.

name: Greek Archaic Sculpture
d: Freestanding kouroi and kore, stiff-legged and smiling enigmatically, brought Egyptian-inspired stone carving into a distinctly Greek idiom of idealized youth.

name: Greek Black-Figure Vase Painting
d: Silhouetted figures incised with fine detail and set against orange clay told myths of gods and heroes on Athenian export pottery that flooded Mediterranean markets.
w: Exekias, Achilles and Ajax playing dice, c. 540 BCE

name: Greek Classical Sculpture
d: Phidias and Polykleitos codified an ideal of balanced contrapposto and mathematical proportion in marble and bronze, embodying the humanist confidence of democratic Athens.

name: Greek Red-Figure Vase Painting
d: Reversing the black-figure technique let painters render anatomy and drapery with fluid brushed lines instead of incision, achieving unprecedented depth and movement.

name: Hellenistic Sculpture
d: After Alexander's conquests scattered Greek culture across three continents, sculptors chased emotional extremity and swirling movement over classical restraint.
w: Laocoon and His Sons, c. 200-70 BCE

name: Etruscan Tomb Painting
d: Tarquinia's underground chambers were painted with lively banquets, dancers, and musicians in flat bright color, celebrating this life to accompany the dead into the next.
w: Tomb of the Leopards, c. 480 BCE
Tomb of Hunting and Fishing, c. 520 BCE

name: Etruscan Bronze and Terracotta Sculpture
d: Master bronze-casters produced the shaggy, wide-eyed Capitoline Wolf and reclining terracotta married couples atop sarcophagi, a warmer naturalism than either Greece or early Rome.
w: Sarcophagus of the Spouses, c. 520 BCE

name: Roman Republican Portrait Sculpture
d: Following an ancestral wax-mask tradition, Republican patricians demanded brutally veristic portraits - every wrinkle and wart intact - to project moral gravitas and lineage.
w: Head of a Roman Patrician, c. 75 BCE

name: Roman Imperial Relief Sculpture
d: State monuments turned relief carving into political propaganda - continuous spiraling narratives of conquest and idealized imperial piety wrapped around columns and altars.
w: Column of Marcus Aurelius, c. 180 CE

name: Roman Wall Painting (Pompeian Styles)
d: Villa walls near Naples were transformed with illusionistic architecture, mythological panels, and moody still lifes, preserved almost intact by Vesuvius's ash in 79 CE.
w: Villa of the Mysteries frieze, c. 60 BCE
House of the Vettii paintings, Pompeii
Garden Room, Villa of Livia, c. 30 BCE

name: Roman Mosaics
d: Floors across the empire, from Tunisian villas to Sicily, were paved with tessellated hunting scenes, personified seasons, and gladiatorial games in millions of tiny stone and glass cubes.
w: Alexander Mosaic, House of the Faun, Pompeii
Great Hunt mosaic, Piazza Armerina, c. 320 CE

name: Late Antique Roman Art
d: As the empire Christianized and fractured, sculptors abandoned classical naturalism for squat, frontal, hierarchically staring figures that anticipate Byzantine style.
w: Portrait of the Tetrarchs, c. 300 CE

name: Scythian Animal-Style Objects
d: Nomadic steppe warriors buried their dead with gold plaques, belt buckles, and horse trappings twisted into coiled stags, griffins, and predators locked in combat.
w: Pazyryk felt saddle covers, c. 500-300 BCE
Gold pectoral, Tovsta Mohyla kurgan, c. 350 BCE

name: Achaemenid Persepolis Reliefs
d: The ceremonial capital's staircases were carved with an orderly procession of tribute-bearing subject nations, projecting an empire of harmonious multicultural rule.
w: Apadana staircase reliefs, Persepolis, c. 500 BCE
Tomb of Darius I facade, Naqsh-e Rustam

name: Achaemenid Gold and Luxury Objects
d: The Oxus Treasure's winged griffin armlets and miniature gold chariots show a court art of portable wealth, drawing on Egyptian, Greek, and Central Asian motifs alike.
w: Oxus Treasure griffin-headed armlets, 5th-4th century BCE
Rhyton in the form of a winged lion, Achaemenid Persia

name: Sasanian Rock Reliefs
d: Cliff faces at Naqsh-e Rustam were carved with monumental scenes of kings receiving divine investiture or triumphing over captured Roman emperors, reasserting Persian imperial ideology.
w: Investiture of Ardashir I, c. 224-240 CE
Triumph of Shapur I over Valerian, c. 260 CE

name: Sasanian Silver and Metalwork
d: Royal silver plates showing kings hunting lions on horseback circulated as diplomatic gifts along the Silk Road, carrying Sasanian court iconography as far as China and Scandinavia.
w: Plate with a king hunting rams, 4th century CE
Cup of Khosrow I, 6th century CE

name: Shang Dynasty Ritual Bronzes
d: Cast in piece-molds of extraordinary precision, ding tripods and wine vessels bore taotie animal masks used in ancestor-worship rituals that legitimized royal power.
w: Owl-shaped you vessel, Anyang, c. 1200 BCE

name: Zhou Dynasty Bronzes and Jade
d: Bronze vessels grew longer inscriptions recording land grants and clan history, while jade carvers produced disc-shaped bi and tube-shaped cong linking earth and heaven.
w: Zeng Hou Yi bronze bell set, c. 433 BCE

name: Qin Terracotta Army
d: Over 8,000 individualized life-size soldiers, horses, and chariots were buried to guard China's first emperor in death, each face modeled distinctly from a limited set of components.
w: Terracotta Army, Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang, c. 210 BCE

name: Han Dynasty Tomb Art
d: Elite burials were filled with painted lacquerware, incised stone reliefs of daily and mythic life, and jade suits sewn with gold thread meant to preserve the body forever.
w: Jade burial suit of Liu Sheng, c. 113 BCE
Mawangdui painted silk banner, c. 168 BCE
Wu Liang Shrine stone reliefs, c. 151 CE

name: Six Dynasties Buddhist Cave Sculpture
d: As Buddhism spread from Central Asia, colossal Buddhas were carved directly from sandstone cliffs at Yungang and Longmen, their drapery and faces shifting from Gandharan solidity to sinuous Chinese linearity.
w: Yungang Grottoes colossal Buddha, c. 460 CE
Longmen Grottoes, Central Binyang Cave, c. 500-523 CE

name: Tang Dynasty Figure Painting
d: Court painters depicted plump, elegantly robed palace ladies and horses with confident, even brushwork, reflecting a cosmopolitan empire open to Silk Road trade and fashion.
w: Zhang Xuan, Court Ladies Preparing Newly Woven Silk, early 8th c.
Han Gan, Night-Shining White, c. 750 CE

name: Tang Sancai Ceramics
d: Lead-glazed 'three-color' earthenware camels, horses, and tomb guardians in amber, green, and cream splashed glazes captured the Silk Road cosmopolitanism of Chang'an.

name: Song Dynasty Landscape Painting
d: Monumental ink landscapes rendered towering mountains dissolving into mist as metaphors for cosmic order, while Southern Song masters pared compositions down to a single misty branch or fisherman.
w: Fan Kuan, Travelers Among Mountains and Streams, c. 1000 CE
Ma Yuan, Fishing on a Snowy River, c. 1195 CE

name: Song Dynasty Ceramics
d: Imperial kilns pursued subtle monochrome perfection - the crackled blue-green of Ru ware, the pale celadon of Longquan, the sky-blue splash of Jun ware - prized above painted decoration.
w: Ru ware brush washer, c. 1100 CE
Ding ware bowl with incised lotus, 11th century

name: Yuan Blue-and-White Porcelain
d: Jingdezhen kilns combined Chinese porcelain technology with Persian cobalt pigment and Islamic-inspired arabesque design, producing export ware that reshaped ceramic history across Eurasia.
w: Yuan blue-and-white jar with dragon, 14th century

name: Jomon Pottery
d: Among the world's oldest pottery, Middle Jomon 'flame-style' vessels were built up with wildly writhing cord-marked clay rims, serving ritual rather than purely practical ends.

name: Yayoi Bronze Dotaku
d: Rice-farming Yayoi communities cast bell-shaped bronze dotaku, decorated with hunting and farming scenes, buried in hillsides for agricultural ritual rather than sounded.
w: Dotaku with hunting scenes, Kagawa, 1st century BCE

name: Kofun Haniwa Sculpture
d: Ringing the huge keyhole-shaped burial mounds of early Japanese chieftains, hollow unglazed clay cylinders evolved into charmingly simplified warriors, horses, and houses.

name: Asuka Period Buddhist Sculpture
d: Japan's first official Buddhist art, imported via Korea, favored archaic almond-eyed smiles and flame-like symmetrical drapery cast in gilt bronze and carved camphor wood.

name: Nara Period Buddhist Sculpture
d: State-sponsored Buddhism reached monumental scale with the bronze Great Buddha of Todai-ji, cast in eight stages, while dry-lacquer and clay techniques gave temple guardians startling realism.

name: Heian Yamato-e Painting
d: Court painters developed a distinctly Japanese narrative style - flattened bird's-eye interiors with roofs removed, thin 'line drawn eyes and hook noses' - to illustrate romantic court novels on hand scrolls.

name: Heian Buddhist Sculpture
d: Sculptor Jocho perfected a joined-woodblock technique enabling serene, gently smiling Amida Buddhas to be mass-produced for Pure Land devotion in gilded temple halls.
w: Amida Buddha, Byodo-in Phoenix Hall, 1053 CE
Kichijoten painted wood statue, Joruri-ji, 12th century

name: Kamakura Period Sculpture
d: Sculptors Unkei and Kaikei revived muscular, crystal-eyed realism for warrior-patron Buddhism, culminating in the ferocious Kongo Rikishi guardians and the outdoor bronze Great Buddha of Kamakura.
w: Kongo Rikishi, Todai-ji South Gate, 1203 CE

name: Three Kingdoms Silla Gold Crowns
d: Silla royal tombs at Gyeongju yielded openwork gold crowns hung with jade curved beads (gogok) and dangling spangles, blending steppe shamanic imagery with dynastic splendor.
w: Gold Crown from Cheonmachong tomb, 5th-6th century
Gold Crown of Silla, Gyeongju National Museum

name: Goguryeo Tomb Murals
d: Chamber tombs near the Goguryeo capitals were painted with vigorous hunting scenes, dancing figures, and the Four Guardian Spirits of the compass directions in bold mineral pigment.
w: Tomb of the Dancers murals, 5th century
Four Guardian Spirits, Tomb of the Four Spirits, 6th century

name: Goryeo Celadon
d: Korean potters perfected a jade-green glaze the Chinese called 'the finest under heaven,' then invented sanggam inlay to press black-and-white slip patterns of cranes and clouds beneath it.
w: Maebyeong vase with inlaid cranes and clouds, 12th century
Celadon incense burner with openwork lid, 12th century

name: Mauryan Ashokan Pillars
d: Emperor Ashoka planted polished sandstone pillars across his realm, each inscribed with edicts of Buddhist dharma and crowned by capitals of confident, Persian-influenced animal sculpture.
w: Lion Capital of Ashoka, Sarnath, c. 250 BCE

name: Gandharan Sculpture
d: At the crossroads of Silk Road trade, Kushan-era sculptors fused Hellenistic drapery and facial features with Buddhist iconography to create the first anthropomorphic images of the Buddha.

name: Mathura School Sculpture
d: Working in warm spotted red sandstone, Mathura's indigenous school gave the Buddha a fleshy, radiant physicality and pioneered the earliest surviving images of Hindu deities.
w: Seated Buddha, Katra Mound, 2nd century CE

name: Gupta Sculpture
d: Often called India's classical age, Gupta sculptors merged Mathura and Gandhara traditions into a serene, transparently-robed Buddha whose downcast eyes and gentle smile became the pan-Asian template.
w: Vishnu reliefs, Udayagiri Caves, c. 400 CE

name: Ajanta Cave Painting
d: Carved deep into a horseshoe cliff, Buddhist monastery caves were painted with sinuous, densely populated Jataka tale murals in tempera, among the finest ancient paintings to survive anywhere in Asia.

name: Pala Bronze and Stone Sculpture
d: Bengal's last great Buddhist dynasty cast lithe, ornately jeweled bronze bodhisattvas at Nalanda that Southeast Asian pilgrims carried home, seeding Buddhist bronze traditions abroad.
w: Black stone stele of Vishnu, 11th century

name: Pala Illuminated Manuscript Painting
d: Palm-leaf Buddhist manuscripts from Vikramashila and Nalanda were illustrated with tiny, jewel-bright painted panels of the Buddha's life, the earliest Indian painting tradition to survive on a portable medium.

name: Chola Bronze Sculpture
d: Using the lost-wax method, Chola founders cast Shiva as Nataraja, cosmic dancer within a ring of fire, a synthesis of dynamic movement and stillness unmatched in world bronze sculpture.
w: Nataraja (Shiva as Lord of the Dance), c. 11th century

name: Khmer Angkor Sculpture and Relief
d: Angkor's temple-mountains were carved with kilometers of narrative bas-relief - churning oceans of milk and battle processions - and populated by serenely smiling four-faced towers under Jayavarman VII.
w: Churning of the Sea of Milk relief, Angkor Wat

name: Javanese Borobudur Relief Sculpture
d: The Sailendra dynasty built the world's largest Buddhist monument as a stepped mandala, wrapping its terraces in nearly 3,000 relief panels guiding pilgrims from earthly desire to enlightenment.

name: Srivijaya Buddhist Bronze Sculpture
d: This maritime empire controlling the Malacca Strait cast softly modeled bronze bodhisattvas that fused Indian Pala grace with local Malay features, spread by monks and traders across the archipelago.

name: Champa Sculpture
d: Cham sandstone towers at My Son sheltered voluptuous, dynamically posed Hindu-Buddhist sculpture, most distinctively the smiling, broad-featured Dong Duong Buddhist style of the 9th century.

name: Olmec Colossal Heads
d: Mesoamerica's 'mother culture' carved multi-ton basalt boulders, hauled from distant quarries, into individualized portrait heads of rulers wearing padded ballgame helmets.
w: Colossal Head 1, San Lorenzo, c. 1200 BCE

name: Teotihuacan Mural Painting
d: The Americas' largest ancient city covered its apartment compounds with brilliant mineral-pigment murals of feathered serpents, jaguars, and a still-unidentified goggle-eyed storm deity.
w: Mural of the Feathered Serpent, Tetitla compound

name: Maya Stone Stelae and Relief Sculpture
d: City-states erected towering carved stelae recording rulers' genealogies, conquests, and calendar rituals in dense hieroglyphic script wrapped around dynamic, richly costumed royal portraits.

name: Maya Polychrome Vase Painting
d: Courtly cylinder vessels were painted with fine-line mythological scenes of the Hero Twins and the underworld, signed by named scribe-painters who held elite courtly status.
w: Vase of the Seven Gods, 8th century

name: Zapotec Funerary Urns
d: Monte Alban's tombs held elaborate effigy urns of seated deities in elaborate headdresses, molded in gray clay to accompany nobles into the afterlife.
w: Bat God effigy urn, Monte Alban

name: Toltec Sculpture
d: Tula's pyramid was crowned by four-story basalt Atlantean warrior columns in feathered headdresses, holding spear-throwers, a militaristic aesthetic later absorbed by the Aztecs as ancestral prestige.
w: Atlantean warrior columns, Pyramid B, Tula, c. 1000 CE

name: Chavin Stone Sculpture
d: A pilgrimage temple complex hid a labyrinth of galleries centered on the Lanzon, a knife-shaped granite idol fusing jaguar, eagle, and human features that spread a shared religious iconography across the Andes.

name: Paracas Textiles
d: Mummy bundles on Peru's desert coast were wrapped in the ancient world's most technically dazzling embroidered textiles, densely packed with rows of flying supernatural figures in vivid dyed camelid wool.
w: Paracas Necropolis embroidered mantle, c. 200 BCE
Paracas Textile, Brooklyn Museum, c. 100 BCE

name: Nazca Ceramics and Geoglyphs
d: Polychrome slip-painted pottery depicted the same hummingbirds, monkeys, and killer whales that Nazca artists also traced at monumental scale as desert-floor geoglyphs visible only from above.
w: Nazca polychrome effigy vessel, 1st-4th century CE
Nazca Lines: Hummingbird and Monkey geoglyphs

name: Moche Portrait Vessels
d: Stirrup-spout ceramic vessels were modeled into astonishingly individualized human portrait heads and narrative scenes of warfare, sacrifice, and sexuality, a naturalism unmatched elsewhere in the ancient Americas.

name: Tiwanaku Monumental Sculpture
d: On the high Bolivian altiplano, Tiwanaku carved massive andesite monoliths and the Gateway of the Sun, its lintel centered on a staff-bearing sky god that became a pan-Andean religious icon.
w: Gateway of the Sun, c. 500-600 CE

name: Wari Textiles
d: The Wari empire's tapestry-woven tunics compressed Tiwanaku's staff-god iconography into abstracted, almost pixelated geometric grids, produced at an industrial scale to clothe an expanding bureaucracy.

name: Chimu Metalwork
d: Chan Chan's mudbrick capital, its walls carved with wave and fish relief friezes, also housed the Andes' finest goldsmiths, who hammered ceremonial tumi knives and beakers of silver and gold alloy.

name: Nok Terracotta Sculpture
d: West Africa's earliest known sculptural tradition modeled hollow, life-sized terracotta heads and figures with pierced pupils and stylized coiffures, their purpose still debated by archaeologists.
w: Nok terracotta head, Jos Plateau, c. 500 BCE

name: Igbo-Ukwu Bronze Objects
d: Centuries before Ife or Benin, a leaded-bronze casting tradition in southeastern Nigeria produced extraordinarily intricate ceremonial vessels, staff ornaments, and regalia covered in filigree-like rope and insect motifs.
w: Igbo-Ukwu bronze roped pot, c. 9th century

name: Ife Bronze and Terracotta Heads
d: The sacred Yoruba city of Ife cast and modeled naturalistic royal heads of astonishing anatomical accuracy in copper alloy and terracotta, a portrait realism unequaled elsewhere in sub-Saharan Africa before modern times.
w: Bronze head with crown, Wunmonije Compound

name: Aksumite Stelae and Coinage
d: The Horn of Africa's trading empire raised towering carved granite stelae mimicking multistory palace facades over royal tombs, and struck some of the first coinage in sub-Saharan Africa, later stamped with the Christian cross.
w: Great Stele of Aksum, c. 300-350 CE
Aksumite gold coin of King Ezana, c. 330 CE

name: Coptic Textiles
d: Egypt's Christian weavers preserved dry desert climate tapestry-woven tunic roundels and clavi bands, blending late-antique classical motifs with new Christian and folk imagery in wool-on-linen.
w: Coptic tapestry roundel with dancing figures, 5th century

name: Early Byzantine Mosaics
d: Glittering gold-ground glass tesserae transformed church interiors at Ravenna and Constantinople into visions of a transcendent, weightless heaven, with Justinian and Theodora depicted as sacred rulers.

name: Byzantine Iconoclasm
d: Imperial decree banned figural religious images for over a century, replacing icons with plain crosses and ornamental motifs on coins, textiles, and church walls until icon veneration was restored in 843.
w: Aniconic cross mosaic, Hagia Irene, 8th century
Iconoclast coinage of Leo III, 8th century

name: Macedonian Renaissance Icon Painting
d: After Iconoclasm's defeat, Constantinopolitan painters revived a softer, more classical humanism in icons and illuminated psalters, folding antique naturalism back into Christian devotional imagery.

name: Palaiologan Renaissance Painting
d: In the empire's final flowering, fresco and mosaic painters at Constantinople's Chora Church achieved a new spatial depth and emotional intensity that would influence early Italian panel painting.
w: Chora Church mosaics of the life of the Virgin

name: Umayyad Art and Architecture
d: The first Islamic dynasty covered the Dome of the Rock and the Great Mosque of Damascus with shimmering gold-ground glass mosaics of jeweled vegetation and empty cities, deliberately avoiding figural imagery in sacred space.
w: Dome of the Rock mosaics, 691 CE
Great Mosque of Damascus mosaics, 715 CE

name: Abbasid Art
d: The new capital at Samarra pioneered carved stucco walls in repeating bevel-cut arabesques and lustreware ceramics that made pottery glint like precious metal, innovations that spread across the Islamic world.

name: Fatimid Art
d: Cairo's Fatimid workshops broke Islamic art's aniconic reserve with luster ceramics, carved rock crystal, and ivory boxes depicting courtly hunting and dancing scenes in a lively, curving line.
w: Fatimid lustre bowl with figure, 11th century

name: Seljuk Art
d: Great Seljuk and Anatolian Seljuk patrons commissioned brilliantly colored mina'i enameled ceramics and inlaid brass vessels with intricate figural and calligraphic bands, alongside monumental brick-and-tile architecture.
w: Mina'i ware bowl with enthronement scene, 12th-13th century

name: Nasrid Art of Granada
d: The Alhambra's palace halls, the last flowering of Islamic Spain, dissolved stone into lace-like carved stucco muqarnas and glazed tile mosaics wrapping courtyards in poetic Arabic inscription.
w: Court of the Lions, Alhambra, c. 1370s
Alhambra tile mosaics and stucco muqarnas

name: Mamluk Art
d: Cairo's sultans and emirs commissioned monumental gilded and enameled mosque lamps of blown glass and inlaid brass basins engraved with elaborate blazons, among the technical high points of medieval Islamic craft.
w: Baptistere de Saint Louis, inlaid brass, c. 1300

name: Timurid Manuscript Painting
d: Under Timurid royal patronage at Herat and Samarkand, book ateliers began fusing Persian and Chinese pictorial conventions into refined manuscript painting that would blossom into the classical Persian miniature.

name: Insular (Hiberno-Saxon) Manuscript Art
d: Irish and Northumbrian monks filled gospel books with impossibly dense full-page 'carpet' pages of interlaced knotwork, spirals, and zoomorphic ornament, treating the sacred text itself as a devotional icon.

name: Merovingian Art
d: Frankish goldsmiths set garnets into cloisonné gold fibulae and sword fittings in dazzling geometric cells, a portable barbarian luxury art bridging Rome's fall and Charlemagne's revival.
w: Childeric I's grave goods, c. 481 CE

name: Carolingian Manuscript Illumination
d: Charlemagne's court scriptoria deliberately revived classical Roman illusionism and script clarity, producing luxurious gospel books with jeweled ivory and gold covers as instruments of imperial and religious renewal.
w: Lorsch Gospels ivory covers, c. 810 CE

name: Ottonian Art
d: Bishop Bernward's monumental bronze doors at Hildesheim, cast in a single piece with narrative reliefs from Genesis to the Passion, revived large-scale figural bronze casting unseen in Europe since antiquity.

name: Viking Art
d: Norse craftsmen carved ships, sledges, and animal-head posts with writhing, ribbon-like interlaced beasts, styles evolving from the Oseberg ship's gripping-beast motifs to the elegant Urnes style's sinuous vines.

name: Romanesque Portal Sculpture
d: Pilgrimage church tympana were carved with dramatically stylized, elongated figures of the Last Judgment, warping proportion and space for maximum spiritual and rhetorical intensity above the doorway.
w: Gislebertus, Last Judgment tympanum, Autun Cathedral, c. 1130

name: Romanesque Wall Painting
d: Catalan and French church apses were painted with a stern, frontal Christ in Majesty within a mandorla, rendered with heavy black outlines and flat color for maximum legibility from a distance.
w: Christ in Majesty, Sant Climent de Taull, 1123 CE

name: Gothic Sculpture
d: Cathedral jamb figures gradually loosened from architectural columns into freestanding, gently swaying bodies with naturalistic drapery and individualized faces, epitomized by the Reims 'smiling angel.'
w: Royal Portal jamb statues, Chartres Cathedral, c. 1145-1155

name: Gothic Stained Glass
d: Ribbed vaulting and flying buttresses freed walls for towering jewel-toned windows, dissolving stone into colored light that told scripture stories in glowing reds and cobalt blues.

name: International Gothic Painting
d: A shared courtly style swept aristocratic Europe from Prague to Paris to Milan, prizing exquisite linear elegance, jewel-like detail, and lavish courtly pageantry over dramatic weight.
w: Limbourg Brothers, Tres Riches Heures du Duc de Berry, begun 1412
Gentile da Fabriano, Adoration of the Magi, 1423

name: Italian Proto-Renaissance Painting
d: Giotto broke from Byzantine flatness to give painted figures weight, emotion, and believable spatial depth on the walls of the Scrovegni Chapel, a foundational rupture that set painting toward the Renaissance.

name: Sienese School Painting
d: Siena's painters prized lyrical line, pattern, and gold-ground elegance over Florentine solidity, from Duccio's shimmering Maestà to Ambrogio Lorenzetti's pioneering city-and-country panorama of good government, before the Black Death abruptly ended the school's golden age.
w: Ambrogio Lorenzetti, Allegory of Good and Bad Government, 1338-1339

name: Ancestral Puebloan Pottery and Architecture
d: Chaco Canyon's great houses and Mesa Verde's cliff dwellings were matched by black-on-white pottery painted with hypnotic geometric hatching, most virtuosically in the figural Mimbres bowls placed over the faces of the dead.
w: Chaco Canyon great house pottery cache

name: Lapita Pottery
d: The first Pacific voyagers to reach Fiji and Tonga stamped their pottery with intricate dentate-toothed geometric and face-like motifs, a shared decorative code marking one of history's greatest maritime migrations.

name: Australian Aboriginal Rock Art
d: On the world's longest continuously practiced artistic tradition, Arnhem Land rock shelters were painted in ochre with dynamic hunting figures, later X-ray style animals showing internal organs and bones, layered generation upon generation.
w: Dynamic Figures rock paintings, Arnhem Land

name: Early Italian Renaissance (Florence)
d: Linear perspective, humanist anatomy, and classical revival transformed Florentine painting from Gothic gold-ground icons into rational, three-dimensional scenes of civic and religious life.

name: High Renaissance (Florence)
d: Leonardo's sfumato and Michelangelo's sculptural figures pushed Florentine painting toward idealized harmony and psychological depth just before the center of gravity shifted to Rome.

name: High Renaissance (Rome)
d: Papal patronage under Julius II and Leo X drew Raphael and Michelangelo to the Vatican, producing the Stanze and the Sistine Ceiling as the era's monumental statements of classical grandeur.

name: Late Renaissance / Venetian School
d: Venetian painters prized color and atmosphere over Florentine drawing, using oil glazes to build luminous, sensuous surfaces in altarpieces and mythological scenes.

name: Early Netherlandish Painting
d: Flemish masters perfected oil glazing to render minutely observed textures, jewels, and light, embedding dense religious symbolism in everyday domestic settings.

name: Northern Renaissance (German)
d: Dürer fused Italian perspective and proportion theory with Gothic precision and printmaking, while Cranach and Holbein sharpened portraiture into incisive psychological record.
w: Hans Holbein the Younger, The Ambassadors, 1533

name: Italian Mannerism
d: After Raphael's death, artists exaggerated elongated figures, unstable compositions, and acidic color into a self-consciously artificial, elegant style that prized invention over naturalism.
w: Parmigianino, Madonna with the Long Neck, 1540
Bronzino, Allegory with Venus and Cupid, 1545

name: School of Fontainebleau
d: Italian artists imported to decorate François I's chateau blended stucco, allegory, and elongated nudes into a courtly French Mannerism that shaped decorative taste for a century.
w: Rosso Fiorentino, Gallery of Francis I, 1535-37
School of Fontainebleau, Gabrielle d'Estrées and one of her Sisters, 1594

name: Italian Baroque Painting
d: Caravaggio's dramatic tenebrism and the Carracci's classicizing naturalism launched a century of theatrical, emotionally charged religious and mythological painting radiating from Rome.
w: Caravaggio, The Calling of Saint Matthew, 1600

name: Spanish Golden Age Painting
d: Under Habsburg patronage, Spanish painters combined Caravaggesque naturalism with austere spirituality and unmatched brushwork, culminating in Velázquez's court portraiture.

name: Flemish Baroque
d: Rubens's workshop produced monumental, muscular, color-saturated altarpieces and mythologies for Counter-Reformation courts across Europe, with Van Dyck refining courtly portraiture.
w: Peter Paul Rubens, Descent from the Cross, 1614
Anthony van Dyck, Charles I at the Hunt, 1635

name: Dutch Golden Age Portraiture
d: A prosperous merchant republic commissioned civic guard group portraits and searching individual likenesses, rendered with psychological candor rather than aristocratic flattery.

name: Dutch Golden Age Still Life
d: Painters catalogued flowers, laid tables, and vanitas skulls with obsessive optical precision, moralizing on abundance and mortality for newly wealthy Dutch households.
w: Willem Kalf, Still Life with a Nautilus Cup, 1662
Rachel Ruysch, Flowers in a Vase, 1690s

name: Dutch Golden Age Landscape
d: Flat polders, windmills, and vast cloud-filled skies were rendered with a new tonal naturalism, celebrating the reclaimed Dutch terrain as national and commercial pride.
w: Jacob van Ruisdael, View of Haarlem, 1670s
Aelbert Cuyp, Distant View of Dordrecht, 1650

name: Dutch Golden Age Genre Painting
d: Quiet domestic interiors — a woman reading a letter, pouring milk, or lit by a window — elevated everyday middle-class life into subjects worthy of jewel-like technical mastery.
w: Johannes Vermeer, Girl with a Pearl Earring, 1665
Pieter de Hooch, Courtyard of a House in Delft, 1658

name: Rococo
d: Pastel colors, curling ornament, and playful pastoral flirtation replaced Baroque gravity, mirroring the pleasure-seeking aristocratic culture of Regency and Louis XV France.
w: François Boucher, The Toilette of Venus, 1751

name: Neoclassicism
d: Reacting against Rococo frivolity and inspired by Pompeii's excavation, painters revived austere classical composition, clear line, and moralizing civic virtue on the eve of revolution.
w: Jacques-Louis David, Oath of the Horatii, 1784

name: Romanticism
d: Painters turned from reason to emotion, the sublime, and the exotic, unleashing turbulent brushwork, dramatic light, and nationalist or nightmarish subject matter.
w: Francisco Goya, The Third of May 1808, 1814
Théodore Géricault, Raft of the Medusa, 1819
Eugène Delacroix, Liberty Leading the People, 1830

name: Realism
d: Courbet and Millet rejected idealized history painting to depict peasants, laborers, and rural life at life-size scale, scandalizing critics who expected only heroic subjects treated so monumentally.

name: Barbizon School
d: Painters settled in the forest village of Barbizon to work directly from nature, prioritizing atmospheric truth over academic idealization and paving the way for Impressionist plein-air practice.
w: Théodore Rousseau, The Forest in Winter at Sunset, 1846-67
Charles-François Daubigny, The Ponds at Gylieu, 1853

name: Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood
d: Rejecting the darkened academic manner descending from Raphael, this English brotherhood painted jewel-bright medieval and literary scenes with photographic botanical detail.

name: Hudson River School
d: America's first native landscape movement painted the Catskills, White Mountains, and western wilderness at panoramic scale, casting untouched nature as evidence of national destiny.
w: Frederic Edwin Church, The Heart of the Andes, 1859
Albert Bierstadt, Among the Sierra Nevada Mountains, 1868

name: Orientalism
d: European painters depicted North Africa and the Ottoman Middle East in richly detailed harems, markets, and deserts, mixing genuine ethnographic curiosity with colonial fantasy.

name: Academic Art / Salon Painting
d: The official Paris Salon rewarded polished, highly finished mythological nudes and history paintings following academic hierarchy of genres — the establishment the avant-garde defined itself against.
w: William-Adolphe Bouguereau, The Birth of Venus, 1879
Alexandre Cabanel, The Birth of Venus, 1863

name: Impressionism
d: Painting outdoors with broken color and visible brushstrokes, this independent group captured fleeting light and modern leisure, rejecting Salon finish in favor of sensation itself.
w: Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Luncheon of the Boating Party, 1881

name: Post-Impressionism
d: Diverging individually from Impressionism, artists pursued structure, symbolic color, and emotional intensity — Cézanne's geometry, Van Gogh's expressive impasto, Gauguin's flattened exoticism.
w: Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night, 1889
Paul Gauguin, Where Do We Come From?, 1897

name: Neo-Impressionism / Pointillism
d: Seurat applied color theory scientifically, juxtaposing tiny dots of pure pigment so the eye would optically blend them into a shimmering, monumentally composed surface.
w: Georges Seurat, A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, 1886
Paul Signac, Portrait of Félix Fénéon, 1890

name: Symbolism
d: Rejecting both naturalism and Impressionist observation, Symbolists painted dreams, myths, and inner psychological states through suggestive, often morbid or mystical imagery.

name: Art Nouveau
d: Whiplash organic curves derived from plant tendrils and female forms swept across posters, ironwork, glass, and architecture, aiming to unify fine and applied art in total design.

name: Arts and Crafts Movement
d: Reacting against industrial mass production, Morris and his circle championed handmade furniture, textiles, and books with medieval-inspired pattern and honest materials.

name: Aestheticism
d: Championing 'art for art's sake,' Whistler and his circle emphasized tonal harmony, decorative arrangement, and beauty over moral or narrative content.
w: James McNeill Whistler, Nocturne in Black and Gold, 1875
Whistler, Arrangement in Grey and Black No.1, 1871

name: Les Nabis
d: Calling themselves 'prophets,' this Paris group flattened color into decorative patterns influenced by Gauguin and Japanese prints, blurring painting into interior design.

name: Les Vingt (Les XX)
d: A Brussels exhibiting society of twenty avant-garde artists gave Symbolism, Neo-Impressionism, and Art Nouveau design their first major platform outside Paris.
w: Fernand Khnopff, I Lock My Door Upon Myself, 1891

name: Peredvizhniki (The Wanderers)
d: Breaking from the Imperial Academy, these Russian realists organized traveling exhibitions of social-critical scenes and psychologically penetrating portraits for provincial audiences.
w: Ilya Repin, Barge Haulers on the Volga, 1873
Ivan Shishkin, Morning in a Pine Forest, 1889

name: Danish Golden Age
d: Copenhagen's Royal Academy under Eckersberg trained a generation to paint clear-eyed, intimate scenes of domestic life, light-filled interiors, and the national landscape.
w: Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg, View through Three Arches, 1815
Christen Købke, View of a Street in Østerbro, 1836

name: Skagen Painters
d: An artists' colony at Denmark's northern tip painted fishermen and luminous blue summer nights en plein air, blending Nordic naturalism with Impressionist light.
w: P.S. Krøyer, Summer Evening on Skagen's Beach, 1893
Anna Ancher, Sunlight in the Blue Room, 1891

name: Macchiaioli
d: Tuscan painters used bold patches ('macchie') of light and shadow to sketch contemporary rural and military life, prefiguring Impressionism outside academic Florence.
w: Giovanni Fattori, The Rotunda of Palmieri, 1866

name: Biedermeier
d: In the politically quiet post-Napoleonic era, Central European middle-class taste favored modest, detailed domestic portraits, interiors, and furniture over grand Romantic gesture.

name: Nazarenes
d: German Romantic painters formed a monastic-style brotherhood in Rome, reviving early Renaissance clarity and devout subject matter against academic convention.

name: Early Renaissance Sculpture
d: Donatello revived classical contrapposto and psychological realism in free-standing bronze and marble, ending medieval sculpture's dependence on architectural niches.

name: High Renaissance Sculpture
d: Michelangelo carved marble with unprecedented anatomical power and emotional depth, treating the block as if liberating a figure already latent within the stone.

name: Baroque Sculpture
d: Bernini fused sculpture, architecture, and light into theatrical ensembles capturing figures at their most dynamic, emotionally charged instant, in marble that seemed to breathe.
w: Gian Lorenzo Bernini, Apollo and Daphne, 1625

name: Neoclassical Sculpture
d: Canova polished marble into smooth, idealized classical forms for European courts, reviving ancient Greek serenity as sculpture's answer to Enlightenment reason.
w: Antonio Canova, Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss, 1793
Bertel Thorvaldsen, Jason with the Golden Fleece, 1803

name: Rodin and the Birth of Modern Sculpture
d: Rodin left surfaces roughly modeled and figures fragmentary, prioritizing raw expressive energy over academic finish, breaking sculpture open for twentieth-century experimentation.
w: Auguste Rodin, The Age of Bronze, 1877

name: Daguerreotype
d: The first commercially viable photographic process fixed a unique, mirror-sharp image on a silvered copper plate, sparking a worldwide portrait-studio craze within a decade.

name: Calotype
d: Talbot's paper negative process allowed multiple positive prints, sacrificing daguerreotype crispness for a softer, more painterly texture and reproducibility.
w: William Henry Fox Talbot, The Pencil of Nature, 1844
David Octavius Hill and Robert Adamson, Newhaven fishwives, 1845

name: Wet Plate Collodion Photography
d: Archer's collodion process combined sharp detail with reproducible glass negatives, becoming the dominant technology for portrait, expedition, and war photography.

name: American Civil War Photography
d: Traveling wet-plate studios documented battlefield dead and army camps with unflinching directness, giving the public its first sustained photographic confrontation with modern war.
w: Alexander Gardner, Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter, 1863

name: Pictorialism
d: Photographers manipulated soft focus, gum bichromate printing, and painterly composition to argue photography was a fine art equal to painting, not mere mechanical documentation.

name: Early Documentary Photography
d: Jacob Riis used magnesium flash photography to expose New York tenement squalor, pioneering photojournalism deployed explicitly for social reform.
w: Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890

name: Muybridge Motion Studies
d: Using rows of trip-wire cameras, Muybridge froze galloping horses and human motion into sequential frames, resolving century-old debates about animal locomotion and seeding cinema.
w: Eadweard Muybridge, Sallie Gardner at a Gallop, 1878

name: Kodak Snapshot Era
d: Eastman's roll-film Kodak camera, marketed 'you press the button, we do the rest,' moved photography out of studios and into the hands of amateurs everywhere.

name: Ming Blue-and-White Porcelain
d: Imperial kilns at Jingdezhen painted cobalt-blue dragons, florals, and landscapes beneath clear glaze, creating export porcelain so coveted it reshaped ceramic traditions across Asia and Europe.

name: Qing Imperial Porcelain
d: Kangxi-era famille verte and Yongzheng/Qianlong famille rose palettes brought unprecedented technical refinement and color range to Jingdezhen's export and imperial wares.

name: Delftware
d: Dutch potters imitated Ming and Wanli porcelain in tin-glazed earthenware, painting blue chinoiserie and Dutch scenes onto plates, tiles, and vases for a booming middle-class market.

name: Meissen Porcelain
d: Europe's first true hard-paste porcelain factory, founded after Böttger cracked the Chinese formula, produced elaborate rococo figurines and services for royal courts.

name: Sèvres Porcelain
d: Under royal and later state patronage, Sèvres perfected soft-paste and hard-paste porcelain with signature ground colors and gilding, becoming the era's diplomatic gift of choice.

name: Wedgwood Jasperware
d: Josiah Wedgwood industrialized fine ceramics, pairing Enlightenment classical taste with unglazed matte jasperware relief in white on colored grounds, marketed via early mass advertising.

name: Chippendale Furniture
d: Thomas Chippendale's pattern book synthesized rococo, Gothic, and Chinese motifs into elegant mahogany chairs and cabinets that defined English cabinetmaking taste.

name: Fabergé
d: Peter Carl Fabergé's workshop crafted bejeweled Imperial Easter eggs and precious objets for the Romanov court, combining goldsmith virtuosity with playful hidden mechanisms.

name: Tiffany Favrile Glass
d: Louis Comfort Tiffany's iridescent Favrile glass and leaded lamps translated Art Nouveau organic form into American decorative art, celebrated at world's fairs.

name: Morris & Co. Textiles
d: William Morris designed dense, nature-derived repeating patterns for wallpaper and woven textiles, insisting on hand-craft and natural dyes against industrial cheapness.

name: Shaker Furniture
d: Shaker communities built spare, functional chairs and cabinets stripped of ornament, believing that honest, well-made work was itself an act of worship.

name: Venetian (Murano) Glass
d: Murano's guild-protected glassmakers invented clear cristallo, filigree, and millefiori techniques, dominating European luxury glass before a 19th-century revival under Salviati.

name: Safavid Carpets
d: Royal Safavid workshops wove silk-and-wool carpets of extraordinary density and intricate arabesque, medallion, and hunting designs for court and mosque.

name: Iznik Ceramics
d: Ottoman potters at Iznik developed a fritware body painted with a signature palette including 'Iznik red,' covering mosque tiles and courtly vessels in dense floral arabesques.
w: Iznik tile panels, Rüstem Pasha Mosque, 1560s

name: Japanese Maki-e Lacquer
d: Artisans built up sprinkled-gold maki-e designs on lacquered wood boxes and furniture, prized domestically and, from the 1600s, as a coveted Nanban export good to Europe.

name: Japanese Netsuke
d: Small ivory or wood toggles used to suspend pouches from a kimono sash evolved into miniature virtuoso carvings of animals, folklore figures, and everyday scenes.
w: Netsuke of a rat, Edo period

name: Islamic Metalwork (Mamluk/Safavid)
d: Mamluk and later Safavid metalworkers inlaid brass and bronze basins, candlesticks, and trays with intricate silver and gold calligraphy and arabesque.

name: Ming Zhe School Painting
d: Court-affiliated professional painters revived vigorous Southern Song academic brushwork in dramatic ink landscapes and figures, contrasting with literati amateur ideals.
w: Wu Wei, Immortal in a Splashed-Ink Landscape, c.1500

name: Ming Wu School Painting
d: Scholar-officials in Suzhou painted restrained, calligraphic literati landscapes for private contemplation, elevating amateur brushwork above professional court painting.

name: Qing Individualist Painters
d: Ming-loyalist monk-painters expressed personal anguish and eccentric vision through radically distorted, expressive brushwork, rejecting Qing-era orthodox conventions.
w: Bada Shanren, Lotus and Ducks, c.1690

name: Qing Orthodox School (Four Wangs)
d: Imperially favored painters systematized past masters' brush techniques into a codified, meticulously layered landscape style that became the Qing academic standard.
w: Wang Hui, The Kangxi Emperor's Southern Inspection Tour, 1698

name: Muromachi Ink Painting (Suibokuga)
d: Zen monk-painters trained in Chinese Song and Yuan models rendered misty landscapes and figures in monochrome ink with spare, meditative brushwork.
w: Josetsu, Catching a Catfish with a Gourd, c.1413

name: Rinpa School
d: Decorative painters used gold-leaf grounds, bold nature motifs, and rhythmic design rather than direct teacher-student lineage, revived across generations from Kōetsu to Hōitsu.
w: Tawaraya Sōtatsu, Wind God and Thunder God, c.1621-25
Ogata Kōrin, Red and White Plum Blossoms, c.1710

name: Kano School
d: This hereditary painting workshop dynasty served shoguns and daimyo for four centuries, producing bold gold-ground screens and formal ink paintings as Japan's official school.

name: Ukiyo-e Woodblock Prints
d: Mass-produced woodblock prints depicted kabuki actors, courtesans, and famous landscapes for a booming urban merchant class, later reshaping Western art through Japonisme.
w: Katsushika Hokusai, The Great Wave off Kanagawa, 1831
Utagawa Hiroshige, One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, 1856-58

name: Nihonga Precursors
d: Responding to Western influence, Fenollosa and Okakura promoted a self-consciously 'Japanese-style painting' synthesizing traditional materials with new compositional ideas.

name: Korean Joseon Painting
d: Court and literati painters developed monochrome ink landscapes and, in the 18th century, a distinctive 'true-view' style depicting actual Korean scenery alongside vivid genre painting.
w: Kim Hong-do, genre album, late 18th c.

name: Mughal Miniature Painting
d: Imperial ateliers under Akbar and Jahangir fused Persian miniature technique with Indian color and European naturalism to produce lavish illustrated manuscripts and portraits.
w: Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings, 1615-18

name: Rajput Painting
d: Independent Hindu courts of Rajasthan commissioned vividly colored, flatter miniatures depicting Krishna legends, court life, and ragamala musical-mode imagery.

name: Pahari (Kangra) Painting
d: Himalayan hill-court painters produced exquisitely lyrical miniatures of Krishna's love for Radha, defined by soft naturalism and delicate line under Nainsukh's influence.

name: Deccani Painting
d: The Deccan sultanates' painters mixed Persian, Turkish, and indigenous Indian idioms into sensuous, richly colored courtly portraits distinct from Mughal restraint.
w: Portrait of Ibrahim Adil Shah II, c.1590

name: Company Painting
d: Indian artists working for British East India Company patrons adapted miniature technique to European taste, cataloguing flora, fauna, castes, and occupations in watercolor.
w: Trades and castes series, Patna, 19th c.

name: Safavid Miniature (Tabriz School)
d: Under Shah Tahmasp's patronage, court painters produced the monumental illustrated Shahnameh, blending Persian and Central Asian traditions in jewel-like detail.
w: Sultan Muhammad, Court of Gayumars, c.1525

name: Safavid Miniature (Isfahan School)
d: After the capital moved to Isfahan, Reza Abbasi pioneered looser, more sensuous single-page drawings of youths and lovers, moving away from manuscript illustration.

name: Ottoman Miniature Painting
d: Topkapı court painters recorded sultans' campaigns and festivals in vivid narrative manuscripts, developing a flatter, more documentary style than Persian miniature.

name: Ottoman Calligraphy
d: Master calligraphers elevated Arabic script into a supreme devotional art form, developing the elegant sülüs and nesih hands used across mosque inscriptions and Qurans.

name: Benin Bronzes
d: Guild casters using lost-wax bronze technique produced commemorative heads, plaques, and altar pieces for the Oba's palace, until British forces looted thousands in 1897.
w: Queen Mother Idia commemorative head, 16th c.

name: Kuba Kingdom Art
d: The Kuba Kingdom produced royal Ndop portrait statues, richly embroidered raffia cut-pile textiles, and elaborately carved ceremonial cups signaling status and lineage.
w: Ndop figure of King Mishe miShyaang maMbul, 18th c.

name: Kongo Art (Nkisi Figures)
d: Kongo carvers made power figures (nkisi nkondi) studded with nails and blades to activate spiritual force, alongside crucifixes blending Catholic and indigenous iconography after Portuguese contact.

name: Asante Goldweights
d: Akan peoples cast small brass weights in figurative and geometric forms to measure gold dust for trade, each shape often encoding a proverb or moral lesson.

name: Ethiopian Icon Painting (Gondar Style)
d: Painters at the new capital of Gondar produced vividly colored icons of saints and biblical narrative for church walls and portable diptychs, defining an enduring Ethiopian Orthodox style.
w: Church mural cycles, Debre Berhan Selassie, 1690s

name: Cusco School
d: Indigenous and mestizo painters in the former Inca capital adapted Spanish Baroque religious imagery with flattened perspective, gold brocade patterning, and local iconographic touches.
w: Cusco school angels with arquebuses, 17th c.

name: Casta Painting
d: Series of sequential canvases in New Spain catalogued mixed-race family groupings and their occupations, ostensibly taxonomic but revealing colonial anxieties about racial hierarchy.

name: Aztec Late Imperial Art
d: Tenochtitlan's sculptors carved monumental stone calendar stones and deity figures in dense, geometric imperial style, integrating cosmology with tribute-empire propaganda before the Spanish conquest.

name: Inca Late Imperial Art
d: Inca artisans produced precisely fitted stone architecture, gold and silver ritual objects, and finely woven checkerboard tunics signaling imperial rank across the Andes.
w: Gold and silver figurines, Machu Picchu era

name: Maori Art (Whakairo)
d: Maori carvers used stone and later steel tools to create intricately interlaced wood carvings for meeting houses and canoes, alongside facial moko tattooing marking genealogy and status.
w: Waka taua (war canoe) prow carvings, 18th c.

name: Hawaiian Featherwork
d: Thousands of tiny bird feathers were knotted onto woven netting to create sacred cloaks, capes, and helmets reserved for ali'i chiefs, signaling divine rank and protection in battle.
w: Kamehameha I feather cloak, late 18th c.

name: Rapa Nui Moai
d: Rapa Nui carvers quarried volcanic tuff to erect monumental ancestor figures on stone platforms, a monumental tradition that ceased amid ecological collapse and social upheaval.
w: Moai of Rano Raraku quarry, 15th c.

name: Northwest Coast Indigenous Art
d: Haida, Tlingit, and Kwakwaka'wakw carvers developed a distinctive formline style of ovoids and curving lines for totem poles, masks, and Chilkat blankets expressing clan crest lineage.

name: Plains Ledger Art
d: Displaced onto reservations and imprisoned, Plains warriors adapted traditional hide-painting narrative to ink and colored pencil on discarded accounting ledger books.

name: Navajo Weaving
d: After Spanish-introduced churro sheep spread wool weaving, Navajo weavers developed banded chief blankets and later elaborate rug patterns using natural and aniline-dyed wool.

name: Fauvism
d: Wild, non-naturalistic color applied in raw slashes and blocks, freed from description of the world; sparked by the 1905 Salon d'Automne room critics dubbed 'the cage of wild beasts.'
w: The Woman with a Hat — Matisse, 1905

name: Die Brücke (Expressionism)
d: Dresden students channeling raw emotion into jagged woodcuts and acid color, rejecting bourgeois academicism for primitivist, urban-anxious imagery.

name: Der Blaue Reiter
d: Munich-based almanac group pursuing spiritual abstraction through color, seeing painting as a path to inner necessity; ended by WWI's mobilization of its members.
w: The Fate of the Animals — Marc, 1913

name: Analytic Cubism
d: Picasso and Braque fractured form into faceted, near-monochrome planes viewed from multiple angles at once, dismantling single-point perspective for good.

name: Synthetic Cubism
d: Cubism's second phase reintroduced color, flatter shapes, and collaged newspaper and wallpaper — papier collé — building images up rather than breaking them down.
w: Still Life with Chair Caning — Picasso, 1912

name: Futurism
d: A manifesto-driven cult of speed, machines, and violence that painted motion itself — dynamism of cars, crowds, and cities — glorifying the industrial future.
w: Dynamism of a Dog on a Leash — Balla, 1912

name: Vorticism
d: Britain's brief answer to Futurism and Cubism, all hard angles and mechanized aggression, broadcast through Wyndham Lewis's typographically explosive magazine Blast.

name: Orphism
d: A lyrical, color-saturated offshoot of Cubism built from overlapping circular prisms of pure hue, named by Apollinaire for its musical, almost mystical abstraction.
w: Simultaneous Windows on the City — Robert Delaunay, 1912

name: Suprematism
d: Malevich reduced painting to pure geometric feeling — a black square, a white square on white — declaring the 'zero of form' as a spiritual and revolutionary act.

name: Constructivism (Painting/Graphics)
d: Revolutionary Russian artists fused geometric abstraction with industrial materials and utilitarian purpose, turning art into propaganda posters, typography, and social engineering — before Stalin suppressed it.
w: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge — Lissitzky, 1919

name: De Stijl
d: Dutch utopians reduced painting to horizontal-vertical grids and primary colors plus black and white, seeking a universal harmony to rebuild culture after WWI.
w: Composition with Red, Yellow, and Blue — Mondrian, 1930

name: Dada (Zurich/Berlin)
d: Born in wartime disgust at Cabaret Voltaire, Dada attacked reason and taste with nonsense sound poems, photomontage, and readymades; Berlin's branch turned it into savage political satire.
w: Cut with the Kitchen Knife — Höch, 1919

name: Dada (New York)
d: Duchamp, Picabia, and Man Ray turned wartime New York into a laboratory of irony, mocking art's seriousness with urinals-as-sculpture and mechanomorphic jokes.
w: The Bride Stripped Bare by Her Bachelors, Even — Duchamp, 1915-23

name: Surrealism
d: Breton's manifesto unleashed the unconscious through automatism, dream imagery, and uncanny juxtapositions, becoming the century's most globally exported avant-garde.

name: Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity)
d: A cold, unsparing realism that dissected Weimar Germany's profiteers, cripples, and cabarets with surgical precision — crushed when the Nazis branded it degenerate.
w: Portrait of the Journalist Sylvia von Harden — Dix, 1926

name: Precisionism
d: America's homegrown modernism celebrated factories, grain elevators, and skyscrapers in crisp, near-abstract geometric clarity, treating industry as sublime.

name: Harlem Renaissance
d: A flowering of Black visual art, literature, and music centered in Harlem that asserted a modern, self-defined African American identity against caricature and erasure.
w: Aspects of Negro Life — Aaron Douglas, 1934

name: Mexican Muralism
d: State-commissioned monumental frescoes by Los Tres Grandes told Mexico's revolutionary history to a mostly illiterate public, fusing folk imagery with Renaissance scale and socialist politics.

name: Social Realism (US)
d: Depression-era painters depicted breadlines, strikes, and factory labor with gritty sympathy, often funded by New Deal art programs.

name: Socialist Realism (USSR)
d: The Soviet state's mandated style — heroic workers, beaming leaders, idealized industry rendered in academic realism — enforced as the only permissible art for six decades.
w: Worker and Kolkhoz Woman — Vera Mukhina, 1937 (sculpture, emblematic)
Stalin and Voroshilov in the Kremlin — Gerasimov, 1938

name: American Regionalism
d: Rural Midwestern life rendered in sturdy, illustrative realism as a nationalist rejoinder to European modernism during the Depression years.
w: A Social History of Missouri — Thomas Hart Benton, 1936
Baptism in Kansas — John Steuart Curry, 1928

name: Abstract Expressionism
d: New York became the center of the art world as Pollock's dripped skeins and de Kooning's slashing figures made gesture itself the subject, prizing scale, spontaneity, and the sublime.

name: Color Field Painting
d: Vast, soaked or floated fields of unmodulated color aimed to absorb the viewer bodily, trading Abstract Expressionism's angst for meditative, near-sublime scale.

name: Art Informel / Tachisme
d: Europe's postwar gestural abstraction — thick impasto, blots, and scrawled marks — channeled trauma into anti-geometric, anti-rational painting.

name: CoBrA
d: Artists from Copenhagen, Brussels, and Amsterdam painted childlike, monstrous figures in raw color, prizing spontaneous experimentation over Parisian sophistication.

name: Gutai
d: Osaka's radical collective made 'concrete' encounters with matter — rolling in mud, throwing paint-filled bottles, running through paper screens — anticipating performance and installation art worldwide.

name: Neo-Dada
d: Rauschenberg's combines and Johns's flags and targets reintroduced everyday objects and ironic detachment into painting, bridging Abstract Expressionism and Pop.

name: Pop Art (US)
d: Warhol's silkscreened soup cans and Lichtenstein's blown-up comic panels turned consumerism and mass media into flat, deadpan, endlessly reproducible art.

name: Pop Art (British)
d: London's Independent Group first theorized Pop through collages celebrating American ads and appliances viewed with fascinated distance rather than American brashness.
w: Just What Is It that Makes Today's Homes So Different, So Appealing? — Hamilton, 1956
Self Portrait with Badges — Peter Blake, 1961

name: Op Art
d: Optical tricks of vibrating lines, moiré grids, and stark contrast made the retina itself the artwork's site, popularized by MoMA's 1965 'The Responsive Eye.'

name: Minimalism (Painting)
d: Stripes, grids, and repeated modules stripped painting of gesture, illusion, and metaphor, insisting the canvas is only what it literally is.
w: Ten Characters — Sol LeWitt wall drawings, from 1968

name: Conceptual Art
d: The idea replaced the object as the artwork, delivered through language, instructions, and documentation — art that could exist as a sentence or a photograph of an event.
w: Paragraphs on Conceptual Art — Sol LeWitt, 1967

name: Arte Povera
d: Italian artists used 'poor' materials — coal, rags, twigs, live plants — to challenge industrial consumer culture with raw, process-based, anti-monumental works.

name: Fluxus
d: An anti-art network of scores, event-objects, and absurdist performances launched at the 1962 Wiesbaden festival, dissolving boundaries between art and everyday action.
w: One Year Performance (Time Clock Piece) precursors — Fluxus scores, 1960s

name: Performance / Body Art
d: Artists made their own bodies the material and site of the work — enduring pain, exhaustion, or vulnerability live before an audience — a practice still central to contemporary art.

name: Photorealism
d: Painters used photographs and projectors to render storefronts, cars, and portraits with hyper-detailed, emotionally cool precision that out-did the camera at its own game.

name: Neo-Expressionism
d: A furious return to big, brushy, figurative painting and mythic subject matter after a decade of Conceptualism's austerity, led by German and American painters alike.

name: Transavanguardia
d: Italy's answer to Neo-Expressionism, named by critic Achille Bonito Oliva, mixed historical styles and myth into eclectic, unabashedly painterly canvases.

name: Neue Wilde (Junge Wilde)
d: Cologne and Berlin's 'young wild ones' painted fast, garish, deliberately crude urban scenes, rebelling against both Conceptual restraint and their Neo-Expressionist elders.

name: Graffiti / Street Art
d: Subway tags and spray-can throw-ups from the Bronx and Brooklyn grew into a global visual language, crossing from vandalism into galleries and, later, sanctioned murals worldwide.

name: Young British Artists (YBA)
d: Goldsmiths graduates backed by collector Charles Saatchi shocked with pickled sharks, unmade beds, and dot paintings, dominating the 1997 'Sensation' exhibition and tabloid headlines alike.
w: The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living — Damien Hirst, 1991
Away from the Flock — Damien Hirst, 1994

name: Neo-Geo
d: A cool, ironic revival of geometric abstraction and commodity imagery that treated Wall Street-era consumer culture with detached, glossy critique.

name: Relational Aesthetics
d: Defined by curator Nicolas Bourriaud, this practice made human interaction itself the artwork — free curry dinners, ping-pong tables, conversation — art as social encounter.

name: Stuckism
d: A deliberately anti-conceptual, pro-painting protest movement founded by Billy Childish and Charles Thomson, mocking the YBA establishment with figurative painting manifestos.
w: The Stuckists Punk Victorian — group show, 2004
Paintings against conceptualism — Billy Childish, ongoing

name: Zaria Art Society (Zaria Rebels)
d: Students at Nigeria's Zaria college rejected their British curriculum's Western focus, forging a 'natural synthesis' that fused Uli line-work and Nok forms with modernist technique on the eve of independence.
w: Ana Mmuo (Land of the Dead) — Uche Okeke, 1961
Christ Carrying the Cross — Demas Nwoko, 1960s

name: Ethiopian Modernism
d: Addis Ababa's new fine arts school produced a generation, led by Skunder Boghossian, blending Coptic manuscript imagery and Amharic magic scrolls with Parisian abstraction — cut short by the 1974 revolution.
w: Night Flight of Dread and Delight — Skunder Boghossian, 1964
The Meskel Flower — Afewerk Tekle, c. 1960s

name: Bengal School of Art
d: Abanindranath Tagore led a nationalist revival drawing on Mughal miniatures and Ajanta murals in soft wash technique, deliberately rejecting British academic realism.
w: Shiva Drinking the Poison — Nandalal Bose, 1930s

name: Progressive Artists' Group (Bombay)
d: Founded the year of independence by six artists including Souza, Husain, and Raza, the group broke from the Bengal School's revivalism to paint with 'absolute freedom,' fusing Indian subject matter with European modernism.
w: Man and Woman Laughing — F.N. Souza, 1957
Between the Spider and the Lamp — S.H. Raza, 1956

name: Cynical Realism
d: After Tiananmen, painters rendered bald, laughing or blank-faced figures in flat, garish color to voice disillusionment with politics and history, a term coined by critic Li Xianting in 1992.

name: Political Pop
d: Wang Guangyi and peers collided Cultural Revolution propaganda imagery with Western consumer logos, mocking both ideologies with the same deadpan poster style.
w: Chairman Mao / Marilyn juxtapositions — various, early 1990s

name: Contemporary Chinese Ink Art
d: Artists reinvented traditional brush-and-ink painting with abstraction, installation, and conceptual strategies, asserting a distinctly Chinese contemporary idiom validated by the Met's 2013 'Ink Art' show.
w: Book from the Sky — Xu Bing, 1987-91

name: Brazilian Concrete Art
d: São Paulo's Grupo Ruptura and Rio's Grupo Frente pursued rigorous, mathematically ordered geometric abstraction inspired by European Concrete art and Brazil's modernizing optimism.
w: Ruptura Manifesto — Waldemar Cordeiro et al., 1952

name: Neo-Concrete Movement
d: Rio dissidents broke from Concretism's rationalism, declaring art a 'quasi-corpus' meant to be touched and inhabited, birthing participatory objects that dissolved the line between painting and body.

name: Madí Movement
d: Buenos Aires avant-gardists broke the rectangular canvas itself, making irregularly shaped, brightly colored geometric paintings that treated the frame as part of the composition.
w: Marco recortado (Cut Frame) works — Rhod Rothfuss, late 1940s

name: Papunya Tula (Western Desert Art)
d: Aboriginal elders at a remote Northern Territory settlement, encouraged by teacher Geoffrey Bardon, translated sacred sand and body-painting designs into acrylic dot paintings on board, launching the modern Aboriginal art movement.
w: Honey Ant Dreaming mural — Papunya school, 1971
Straightening Spears at Ilyingaungau — Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri, 1972

name: Hurufiyya Movement
d: Post-colonial Arab and Iranian modernists deconstructed Arabic calligraphy's letterforms into abstract composition, asserting a culturally rooted alternative to imported Western abstraction.
w: Al-Hurufiyya series — Shakir Hassan Al Said, 1960s-80s

name: Saqqakhaneh Movement
d: Tehran artists mined popular Shi'a folk imagery — votive locks, talismans, coffeehouse painting — fusing vernacular religious culture with modernist abstraction until the 1979 revolution.

name: Soviet Nonconformist Art
d: Underground painters worked in apartments and forests outside state control, developing abstraction and conceptual irony banned from public view — bulldozed literally in 1974 when police crushed an open-air show.
w: Answers of an Experimental Group — Ilya Kabakov, 1970s

name: Digital / NFT / AI Art
d: Blockchain-verified digital images and, later, text-to-image AI generators turned code and algorithms into an art market of their own, epitomized by Beeple's $69 million NFT sale at Christie's.

name: Post-Internet Art
d: Artists treated the internet as a cultural condition rather than a tool, making sculpture, painting, and performance saturated with the aesthetics of stock photos, branding, and social media feeds.
w: The Persistence of Chaos — Guo O Dong, 2017 (later work)

name: Metaphysical Painting (Pittura Metafisica)
d: De Chirico's eerily empty piazzas, long shadows, and mannequin figures conjured an uncanny stillness that directly seeded Surrealism a decade later.
w: The Song of Love — de Chirico, 1914
The Enigma of a Day — de Chirico, 1914

name: Purism
d: Le Corbusier and Ozenfant's manifesto 'Après le cubisme' called for cool, machine-precise still lifes of bottles and glasses, purging Cubism of decorative excess.
w: Still Life with Pile of Plates — Le Corbusier, 1920
Verre, bouteille, paquet de tabac — Ozenfant, 1922

name: Vienna Actionism
d: Nitsch, Muehl, Brus, and Schwarzkogler staged visceral, blood-and-flesh rituals attacking Catholic guilt and postwar Austrian repression, pushing body art to its most extreme edge.
w: Orgies Mysteries Theatre actions — Hermann Nitsch, from 1962

name: Feminist Art Movement
d: Judy Chicago and Miriam Schapiro's CalArts Feminist Art Program and the collaborative Womanhouse installation reclaimed craft, the body, and domestic space as serious subject matter.
w: Semiotics of the Kitchen — Martha Rosler (video), 1975

name: Appropriation Art
d: Artists re-photographed or re-painted existing images wholesale — ads, film stills, master paintings — to interrogate authorship, originality, and image saturation under postmodernism.
w: Equivalent VIII appropriations debate — surrounding readymade discourse, 1980s

name: Chicano Art Movement
d: Rising alongside the Chicano civil rights movement, muralists and collectives like ASCO painted barrio walls with Aztec, Catholic, and pop-culture imagery asserting Mexican-American identity.
w: La Historia de California — East LA muralists, 1970s

name: Superflat
d: Takashi Murakami's manifesto linked anime and manga's flat, hyper-decorative surfaces to historical Japanese art, blurring high art and otaku pop culture into a single 'superflat' plane.

name: Outsider Art / Art Brut
d: Dubuffet championed self-taught, institutionalized, or visionary makers working entirely outside art-world training, prizing raw, unfiltered creative compulsion over technique.
w: Collection de l'Art Brut holdings — various self-taught artists, opened 1976
Untitled works — Henry Darger, mid-20th c.

name: Video Art
d: Nam June Paik's first Portapak recordings launched a medium that let artists manipulate, loop, and distort broadcast television's own language, now a staple of biennials and museum galleries.

name: Zero (Group)
d: Düsseldorf artists sought a 'zero point' after the war's devastation — pure light, vibration, and monochrome nail-fields — networking with kindred groups across Europe and Latin America.

name: Support/Surfaces
d: French artists dismantled painting into its material components — unstretched canvas, dyed fabric, raw wooden stretcher bars — displayed as separate, deconstructed elements.
w: Untitled (dyed canvas works) — Claude Viallat, from 1966

name: Kinetic Art (GRAV)
d: Paris's Groupe de Recherche d'Art Visuel built optical and mechanically moving works meant to be touched and activated by viewers, democratizing art through participation and motion.

name: Rodin's Late Legacy
d: Rodin's rough, unfinished-looking bronze surfaces and fragmentary bodies, radical for their expressive emotion over academic polish, set the template every 20th-century sculptor reacted to.
w: The Gates of Hell — Rodin, worked until his death, 1917

name: Brancusi & Modernist Sculpture
d: Brancusi pared the figure down to gleaming, near-abstract essential forms — an egg, a fish, a bird in flight — arguing that simplicity itself was reality.

name: Futurist Sculpture
d: Boccioni translated Futurist dynamism into bronze, dissolving the figure into the force-lines of its own motion through space.
w: Unique Forms of Continuity in Space — Boccioni, 1913
Development of a Bottle in Space — Boccioni, 1912
Fusion of a Head and a Window — Boccioni, 1912

name: Constructivist Sculpture
d: Tatlin and Gabo built with industrial materials — wire, glass, sheet metal — proposing sculpture as engineering, most famously an unbuilt spiraling tower meant to outdo the Eiffel Tower.
w: Monument to the Third International (model) — Tatlin, 1919-20

name: Giacometti & Existential Figuration
d: Postwar Giacometti made impossibly thin, scarred bronze figures that seemed to be dissolving under the viewer's gaze, embodying existentialist isolation and fragility.

name: Calder & the Mobile
d: Calder invented the hanging mobile — abstract shapes in perfect wind-driven balance — turning sculpture from static mass into playful, ever-changing motion.
w: Lobster Trap and Fish Tail — Calder, 1939

name: Minimalist Sculpture
d: Industrially fabricated boxes, stacks, and floor pieces in raw metal and plywood rejected pedestal, narrative, and the artist's hand, foregrounding the viewer's own bodily experience of space.

name: Land Art / Earthworks
d: Artists left the gallery entirely, cutting, mounding, and spiraling the American desert itself into monumental, slowly eroding sculptures visible only from the air or after a long drive.

name: Installation Art
d: Whole rooms became the artwork — immersive, often walk-through environments of light, sound, and object — evolving from Kaprow's 1950s 'Environments' into today's dominant contemporary mode.
w: Infinity Mirror Rooms — Yayoi Kusama, ongoing since 1965

name: Contemporary Monumental Sculpture
d: Kapoor's mirrored voids and Kusama's polka-dotted pumpkins scaled sculpture up to plaza-filling, Instagram-magnet public spectacle, blending sublime abstraction with mass popularity.

name: Assemblage / Junk Sculpture
d: Nevelson's monochrome wooden walls and Chamberlain's crushed automobile bodies turned discarded urban debris into monumental, painterly sculpture.

name: New British Sculpture
d: A generation after Caro turned to industrial materials, ordinary objects, and the cast human body — Gormley's body-casts, Cragg's assembled plastics — to renew figurative and material sculpture.
w: Britain Seen from the North — Tony Cragg, 1981

name: Mono-ha
d: Tokyo artists arranged raw stone, steel, wood, and earth in near-untouched states, presenting materials 'as they are' in dialogue with each other rather than transformed by the artist's hand.

name: Photo-Secession
d: Stieglitz's invitation-only society and his journal Camera Work and Gallery 291 institutionalized art photography in America and later introduced European modern art to US audiences.

name: Straight Photography / Group f/64
d: West Coast photographers rejected Pictorialist softness for sharp focus, full tonal range, and unmanipulated prints of nature and everyday objects, founding a manifesto group in 1932.
w: Monolith, the Face of Half Dome — Ansel Adams, 1927

name: New Vision / Bauhaus Photography
d: Moholy-Nagy's 'New Vision' pushed cameraless photograms, extreme angles, and double exposures, treating the camera as a tool for radically re-training human perception.

name: Surrealist Photography
d: Man Ray's cameraless rayographs and solarized nudes, alongside Brassaï's nocturnal Paris, used the darkroom itself to produce uncanny, dreamlike distortions of reality.

name: FSA Documentary Photography
d: A federal photography unit under Roy Stryker sent Lange, Evans, and others to document Depression-era rural poverty, producing some of the century's most iconic and politically consequential images.
w: Bud Fields and His Family — Walker Evans, 1936

name: Magnum Photojournalism
d: Founded by Capa, Cartier-Bresson, Seymour, and Rodger as a photographer-owned cooperative, Magnum defined mid-century photojournalism's ethical, on-the-ground eyewitness style and remains active today.

name: Subjective Photography (Subjektive Fotografie)
d: Otto Steinert's touring exhibitions championed a personal, experimental postwar German photography of abstraction and expressive form, reviving avant-garde technique after Nazi-era conservatism.

name: The Family of Man Era
d: Edward Steichen's MoMA mega-exhibition of 503 photographs from 68 countries argued for a universal human family, becoming the most-seen photography show ever, while later critics attacked its Cold War humanism as naive.
w: The Family of Man exhibition prints — curated by Steichen, 1955
Nursing mothers sequence — various photographers, 1955 exhibition

name: Street Photography (New York School)
d: Winogrand, Friedlander, and Arbus roamed the city with handheld 35mm cameras, capturing candid, off-kilter, often unflattering slices of American public life.
w: Identical Twins, Roselle, New Jersey — Diane Arbus, 1967

name: New Topographics
d: A landmark 1975 Rochester exhibition presented deadpan, large-format photographs of parking lots, tract housing, and industrial sprawl, redefining landscape photography around the 'man-altered' environment.
w: New Topographics exhibition prints — group show, 1975

name: Düsseldorf School of Photography
d: Bernd and Hilla Becher's typological, deadpan grids of industrial structures trained a generation at the Düsseldorf academy who scaled photography up to painting-sized, hyper-detailed grandeur.
w: Water Towers — Bernd and Hilla Becher, 1972-2009

name: Color Photography's Fine-Art Acceptance
d: William Eggleston's dye-transfer prints of Memphis gas stations and dinner tables, shown at MoMA in 1976, ended decades of art-world snobbery that had confined color to advertising and snapshots.

name: Fashion Photography
d: From Horst's glamorous studio lighting to Avedon's stark white backdrops and kinetic models, fashion photography became a major art form in its own right, shaping and reflecting each decade's ideal image.
w: Woman in Moroccan Palace — Irving Penn, 1951

name: Conceptual Photography (Pictures Generation)
d: A cohort raised on television and advertising staged, restaged, and appropriated media imagery to question identity and authorship, launched by Douglas Crimp's 1977 'Pictures' exhibition.
w: Untitled (We Won't Play Nature to Your Culture) — Barbara Kruger, 1983

name: Digital Photography Transition
d: Digital sensors replaced film across professional and consumer photography within a decade and a half, upending darkroom craft, newspaper workflows, and photographic archives worldwide.
w: Consumer digital camera boom — various manufacturers, 1995-2005
Digital photojournalism transition — major wire services, early 2000s

name: Smartphone / Social Image Era
d: The iPhone camera and apps like Instagram made everyone a photographer and publisher simultaneously, collapsing the distance between taking a picture and broadcasting it to the world instantly.

name: Art Deco
d: Sleek geometric ornament, exotic materials, and streamlined luxury defined interwar design from Paris jewelry to New York skyscrapers, crystallized by the 1925 Exposition des Arts Décoratifs.
w: Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs objects — Paris, 1925

name: Bauhaus Design
d: Gropius's school fused fine art, craft, and industry into functionalist tubular-steel furniture, geometric typography, and modular housing — closed by the Nazis but scattered its faculty worldwide.

name: Streamline Moderne
d: Industrial designers borrowed aerodynamic teardrop curves from airplanes and locomotives to reshape toasters, radios, and diners for a Depression-era public hungry for the future.
w: Coldspot Super Six refrigerator — Raymond Loewy, 1935
Twentieth Century Limited locomotive — Henry Dreyfuss, 1938

name: Scandinavian Modern
d: Danish, Swedish, and Finnish designers married functionalist restraint with warm woods and human-centered ergonomics, exported worldwide by the touring 'Design in Scandinavia' show.

name: Mid-Century Modern
d: Postwar optimism and new materials like molded plywood and fiberglass produced organic, mass-producible furniture for the booming suburban home, epitomized by California's Case Study Houses.
w: Eames Lounge Chair — Charles and Ray Eames, 1956

name: Memphis Group / Italian Radical Design
d: Ettore Sottsass's collective smashed modernist 'good taste' with clashing patterns, plastic laminate, and deliberately garish, cartoonish furniture — postmodernism's design manifesto.

name: Studio Glass Movement
d: Harvey Littleton's small-scale furnace workshops at the Toledo Museum let individual artists blow glass outside factory settings for the first time, birthing glass as a studio fine-art medium.

name: British Studio Pottery
d: Bernard Leach's St Ives pottery, built with Japanese potter Hamada Shoji, fused East Asian glazing and form with English folk tradition, codified in his influential 1940 'A Potter's Book.'
w: Leaping Salmon vase — Bernard Leach, c. 1930s
Standard ware — Leach Pottery, ongoing production

name: American Studio Ceramics
d: Peter Voulkos at LA's Otis Art Institute smashed, gouged, and stacked clay with Abstract Expressionist bravado, arguing ceramics could be sculpture rather than craft.

name: Japanese Mingei (Folk Craft) Movement
d: Philosopher Yanagi Sōetsu championed anonymous everyday folk crafts — pottery, textiles, baskets — as holding a truer beauty than elite fine art, founding the Japan Folk Crafts Museum in 1936.
w: Japan Folk Crafts Museum collection — founded 1936
The Unknown Craftsman (book) — Yanagi Sōetsu, 1972 (posthumous compilation)

name: Contemporary Craft Revival
d: A 21st-century resurgence of hand-making — studio furniture, artisanal ceramics, textile art — pushed back against mass production, fueled by maker culture, craft fairs, and social media visibility.
w: Loewe Craft Prize submissions — various, from 2016
Contemporary ceramics market growth — global craft fairs, 2010s

name: Industrial/Product Design Icons
d: Dieter Rams's 'ten principles of good design' at Braun distilled function into minimalist white and grey consumer electronics, a philosophy later echoed directly in Apple's global product design.
